u:sd-5-sql-vs-nosql-choosing-a-db.summary: Match the datastore to consistency needs, scale, and access patterns.

rows: High scale, flexible data, simple access patterns

blocks.text: Choose SQL for structured data needing strong consistency and complex queries (payments, orders). Choose NoSQL for massive scale, flexible schemas, or specific access patterns (feeds, catalogs, sessions). It's a fit decision; large systems are often polyglot.
In an interview, justify the DB choice from the requirements (consistency? scale? query shape?) rather than naming a favourite product.

mcqs.q: A workload needing strong consistency and complex multi-table joins suits:
mcqs.explain: SQL databases provide ACID transactions and rich joins for structured, consistency-critical data.

mcqs.q: NoSQL databases are typically chosen for:
mcqs.explain: NoSQL targets scale and schema flexibility, often trading some consistency and join power.

mcqs.q: The right SQL vs NoSQL choice is driven by:
options: The workload's consistency, scale, and query requirements
mcqs.explain: It's a requirements-driven fit decision, not a fashion choice.

u:sd-6-database-indexing.title: Database Indexing
u:sd-6-database-indexing.summary: Trade write speed and storage for dramatically faster reads on indexed columns.

blocks.text: An **index** is a data structure (usually a **B+ tree**) that speeds up lookups on a column, turning a full-table scan into a logarithmic search. It's the single biggest lever for query performance.

items: Great for columns in **WHERE**, **JOIN**, and **ORDER BY** clauses.
**Costs**: extra storage and slower writes (every write updates the indexes).
A **composite index** covers multiple columns (order matters — leftmost prefix rule); a **covering index** contains all columns a query needs (index-only scan).

blocks.text: Index read-heavy query paths, not everything: indexes speed reads but slow writes and use space. Low-selectivity columns (few distinct values) and write-heavy tables often don't benefit. Wrapping a column in a function disables its index.

mcqs.q: Database indexes primarily improve:
options: Read/query speed on the indexed columns
mcqs.explain: Indexes turn scans into fast lookups for reads, at the cost of write speed and storage.

mcqs.q: A cost of adding many indexes is:
options: Slower writes (each write updates every index) and more storage
mcqs.explain: Every insert/update/delete must maintain all indexes, and indexes consume space.

mcqs.q: Most relational indexes are implemented as:
mcqs.explain: B+ trees give logarithmic lookups and efficient range scans, the default index structure.

u:sd-7-database-replication-master-slave.title: Database Replication (Master-Slave / Master-Master)
u:sd-7-database-replication-master-slave.summary: Copy data across nodes for read scaling and availability, with different write topologies.

blocks.text: **Replication** keeps copies of data on multiple nodes for **read scaling** and **high availability** (failover).

rows: One primary handles writes; replicas serve reads
Higher write availability; risk of write conflicts

blocks.text: Master-slave scales reads and gives failover but funnels writes to one primary (a bottleneck / single point for writes). Master-master allows writes on multiple nodes (better write availability) but must resolve conflicting concurrent writes. Replicas can lag, so reads may be slightly stale.
Replication lag means a just-written value may not appear on a replica immediately — handle 'read-your-writes' by reading from the primary when it matters.

mcqs.q: In master-slave replication, writes go to:
mcqs.explain: A single primary accepts writes; replicas replicate and serve reads, scaling reads and enabling failover.

mcqs.q: A challenge unique to master-master replication is:
options: Resolving conflicting concurrent writes on multiple primaries
mcqs.explain: Multiple write nodes can accept conflicting writes, requiring conflict resolution.

mcqs.q: Replication lag can cause:
options: A recently written value not yet appearing on a replica (stale reads)
mcqs.explain: Asynchronous replicas may briefly lag, so reads from them can be stale.

u:sd-8-database-sharding-partitioning.title: Database Sharding & Partitioning
u:sd-8-database-sharding-partitioning.summary: Split data across nodes to scale writes and storage — the shard key is everything.

blocks.text: **Sharding (horizontal partitioning)** splits a large dataset across multiple nodes by a **shard key**, so each node holds a subset — scaling **writes** and **storage**.

rows: Ranges of the key per shard
Even spread, but resharding is hard
A lookup table maps keys to shards
Flexible; the directory is a bottleneck/SPOF

blocks.text: The shard key is the critical decision: it must spread load evenly (avoid **hotspots**) and keep most queries on a single shard. **Cross-shard queries and transactions** are expensive — a major cost of sharding. Vertical partitioning (splitting columns/tables) is a different technique.
Choosing a low-cardinality or monotonically increasing shard key (like timestamp) creates hotspots — one shard gets all the recent traffic.

mcqs.q: Sharding primarily scales:
options: Writes and storage by splitting data across nodes
mcqs.explain: Each shard holds a subset, distributing write and storage load.

mcqs.q: The most critical decision in sharding is:
options: Choosing a shard key that avoids hotspots and keeps queries on one shard
mcqs.explain: A poor shard key causes uneven load (hotspots) and forces expensive cross-shard operations.

mcqs.q: A major downside of sharding is:
options: Cross-shard queries and transactions become complex and slow
mcqs.explain: Operations spanning shards are expensive, so designs try to keep each query within one shard.

u:sd-9-cap-theorem.title: CAP Theorem
u:sd-9-cap-theorem.summary: During a network partition, choose consistency or availability — not both.

blocks.text: **CAP** says a distributed store can guarantee at most two of **Consistency**, **Availability**, and **Partition tolerance**. Since partitions are unavoidable in real networks, **P is mandatory** — so the real choice during a partition is **C vs A**.

rows: Stay available; may return stale data

blocks.text: The real reading: because partitions happen, you must pick — be consistent (CP, refuse possibly-stale answers) or available (AP, serve, accepting staleness). 'Pick 2 of 3' really means 'pick C or A when P occurs'.

mcqs.q: During a network partition, CAP forces a choice between:
mcqs.explain: Partition tolerance is required, so the trade-off during a partition is consistency vs availability.

mcqs.q: A CP system during a partition will:
options: Sacrifice availability to stay consistent (reject some requests)
mcqs.explain: CP prioritises consistency, refusing to serve data it can't guarantee is current.

mcqs.q: An AP system like Cassandra during a partition:
options: Stays available but may return stale (eventually consistent) data
mcqs.explain: AP keeps answering, accepting temporary inconsistency.

u:sd-10-pacelc-consistency-models.title: PACELC & Consistency Models
u:sd-10-pacelc-consistency-models.summary: Beyond CAP: even without a partition, you trade latency against consistency.

blocks.text: **PACELC** extends CAP: **if Partition (P)**, choose Availability or Consistency (A/C); **Else (E)** — in normal operation — choose **Latency or Consistency (L/C)**. It captures the everyday trade-off CAP ignores.
Consistency models

rows: Every read sees the latest write (like a single copy)
Replicas converge over time; reads may be stale
Causally-related operations are seen in order
You always see your own updates

blocks.text: PACELC's insight: consistency has a cost even without failures — waiting for replicas to agree adds latency. So systems tune between strong consistency (slower) and eventual consistency (faster, possibly stale). Choose the weakest model that's still correct for your use case.

mcqs.q: PACELC adds to CAP the idea that, even without a partition, you trade:
mcqs.explain: The 'ELC' part: in normal operation, stronger consistency costs more latency.

mcqs.q: Eventual consistency means:
options: Reads always see the latest write
Replicas converge over time and reads may be temporarily stale
mcqs.explain: Updates propagate asynchronously; given no new writes, all replicas eventually agree.

mcqs.q: Strong consistency typically costs:
options: Higher latency (waiting for replicas to agree)
mcqs.explain: Coordinating replicas to guarantee the latest value adds latency, per PACELC.

u:sd-11-consistent-hashing.title: Consistent Hashing
u:sd-11-consistent-hashing.summary: Distribute keys so adding/removing a node moves only ~1/N of them.

blocks.text: With `hash(key) % N`, changing N remaps almost every key — disastrous for caches/shards. **Consistent hashing** maps both nodes and keys onto a hash **ring**; a key belongs to the first node clockwise. Adding/removing a node moves only the keys between it and its neighbour — about **1/N**.

items: **Minimal remapping** when the cluster scales — only ~K/N keys move.
**Virtual nodes** (each server at many ring positions) even out distribution and smooth load when a node fails.
Used by distributed caches, Cassandra, DynamoDB, and sharded systems.

blocks.text: Consistent hashing lets nodes join/leave with minimal reshuffling — the key reason it underpins distributed caches and databases. Virtual nodes fix uneven distribution and hotspots.

mcqs.q: The main advantage of consistent hashing is that adding/removing a node:
mcqs.explain: Only keys near the changed node move (~K/N), versus remapping nearly everything with modulo hashing.

mcqs.q: Virtual nodes in consistent hashing are used to:
options: Even out key distribution and avoid hotspots
mcqs.explain: Placing each server at many ring points balances load and smooths redistribution.

mcqs.q: In consistent hashing, a key is assigned to:
options: The first node clockwise on the ring
mcqs.explain: Keys map to the next node clockwise from their position on the ring.

u:sd-12-message-queues-kafka-rabbitmq.title: Message Queues (Kafka / RabbitMQ)
u:sd-12-message-queues-kafka-rabbitmq.summary: Decouple producers and consumers with an async buffer; know the log vs broker distinction.

blocks.text: A **message queue** lets producers send messages that consumers process asynchronously, **decoupling** them for independent scaling, reliability, and load smoothing.

rows: Smart broker routes/deletes messages after ack
Distributed append-only log; consumers track offsets

blocks.text: Queues turn synchronous coupling into resilient async flow: producers/consumers scale separately, spikes are buffered, and work survives consumer crashes. Kafka (a partitioned log) excels at high-throughput streaming and replay; RabbitMQ (a broker) excels at flexible routing and task queues.
Delivery guarantees: at-least-once (may duplicate → make consumers idempotent) is most common; exactly-once is hardest.

mcqs.q: A message queue's primary benefit is:
options: Asynchronous decoupling of producers and consumers with buffering
mcqs.explain: It lets producers and consumers operate independently, smoothing load and improving reliability.

mcqs.q: Kafka differs from a traditional broker by:
options: Being a distributed append-only log where consumers track offsets and can replay
mcqs.explain: Kafka retains a partitioned log; consumers read at their own offset and can re-read, enabling streaming/replay.

mcqs.q: With at-least-once delivery, consumers should be:
mcqs.explain: At-least-once may deliver duplicates, so processing must be idempotent.
